Name: distributed_redundant_storage
Title: No Single Neuron to Blame: Redundant Distributed Storage of Robust Facts
Short Hypothesis: Highly reliable facts are stored redundantly across multiple MLP modules and layers, so that ablating any single causal-tracing-identified locus fails to erase the fact, whereas fragile facts have a single point of failure. Redundancy count predicts robustness to editing and to noise, refining the localized-vs-distributed debate into a graded per-fact property.
Related Work: ROME/MEMIT edit a single locus and succeed for many facts, implying localization; yet studies show editing is brittle and facts survive some ablations, implying distribution. We reconcile these by proposing per-fact redundancy as the hidden variable, and by measuring how many independent loci must be ablated to erase a fact-a measurement neither localization nor distribution accounts have made.
Abstract: Whether factual knowledge is localized or distributed is often posed as a binary, but evidence cuts both ways: single-locus edits succeed, yet ablations frequently fail to remove facts. We propose that facts differ in storage redundancy-the number of independent components that each suffice to support recall-and that this per-fact quantity, not a global architectural fact, governs the debate. We operationalize redundancy by greedily ablating causally-implicated MLP modules until recall breaks, counting the minimal ablation set. We hypothesize that (i) robust, high-frequency facts require ablating several independent loci, while rare facts break with one; (ii) redundancy predicts resistance to knowledge editing (redundant facts 'snap back'); and (iii) redundancy predicts robustness to activation noise. Across models and a large fact set, we measure redundancy, correlate it with frequency, edit-resistance (post-edit recovery under paraphrase), and noise tolerance. We also test whether redundant loci carry correlated or complementary information via pairwise ablation. This transforms the localized-vs-distributed question into a measurable spectrum and offers a diagnostic for which facts are safely editable and which will resist editing, directly informing model-editing practice.
Experiments: 1. For each fact, run causal tracing to get candidate MLP loci. 2. Greedily ablate loci (zero or mean-patch) until recall probability drops below threshold; record minimal ablation-set size = redundancy. 3. Correlate redundancy with subject frequency. 4. Apply ROME/MEMIT edits and measure paraphrase-robust edit success vs redundancy. 5. Inject Gaussian noise at loci and measure accuracy vs redundancy. 6. Pairwise ablation to test complementarity. Metrics: redundancy count distribution, frequency correlation, edit-success vs redundancy, noise-tolerance curve.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Greedy ablation may overestimate minimal sets; combinatorial search is expensive. Ablation methods (zero vs mean) can give different answers. 'Recall broken' threshold is arbitrary. Redundancy could reflect probe artifacts rather than true storage. Results may be scale-dependent.
